title: Europe needs a new strategy for Russian gray zone aggression
gist: Following von der Leyen's call for a 'counter-hybrid playbook', the authors argue Europe's reactive, unanimity-bound approach cannot deter escalating Russian gray zone aggression. They urge cost-imposing measures: extending the European Sky Shield Initiative over western Ukraine, boarding and potentially seizing shadow-fleet tankers, and finding a legal route to allocate over $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets to Ukraine — while acknowledging escalation and financial-stability risks.

insights.claim: Von der Leyen's call for a 'counter-hybrid playbook' concedes Europe's institutions have failed to keep pace with Russian gray zone aggression, but Brussels' response remains focused on reacting rather than establishing credible deterrence.
insights.so_what: Ongoing hybrid attacks on European infrastructure remain a persistent risk absent deterrence.
insights.quote: managing the aftermath of Russian attacks is neither strategy nor “strategic independence.”
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: EU unanimity requirements mean a single captured government can block collective action against Russia, as has repeatedly happened with sanctions since 2022; a planned European Security Council with Ukraine, the UK, Norway and Canada may not help if all participants hold vetoes.
insights.so_what: Expect continued delays in EU sanctions and collective responses.
insights.locator: The approach envisioned by von der Leyen
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Russia will keep expanding hostile actions until it finds Europe's real red lines, at which point miscalculation on either side becomes a major risk; deterrence will no longer come from strategic restraint.
insights.so_what: Rising tail risk of a direct Russia-Europe incident.
insights.quote: Genuine deterrence will no longer come from strategic restraint.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Europe could extend the European Sky Shield Initiative to cover parts of western Ukraine, framed as a response to Russian violations of NATO airspace, rather than waiting for missiles and drones to cross into EU territory.
insights.so_what: Would expand demand for European air-defense systems and raise escalation risk.
insights.locator: One option would be to help close
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz support a bigger Polish role in Ukrainian air defense so missiles are intercepted before reaching Poland.
insights.so_what: Poland is the likely lead nation for any cross-border air-defense extension.
insights.quote: so that missiles can be intercepted there and do not reach Poland.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Kremlin warnings that intercepting Russian drones over Ukraine would risk direct conflict mirror repeated threats used throughout the invasion to deter support for Ukraine.
insights.so_what: Authors discount Russian escalation threats as bluff-like signaling.
insights.locator: Previous calls to extend air defense coverage
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

themes.theme: Shadow fleet and frozen assets leverage

insights.claim: Europe should enforce shadow-fleet measures more strictly, boarding tankers and detaining crews lacking valid certification or insurance, and explore legal options to move from temporary detention to outright seizure of vessels.
insights.so_what: Stricter enforcement could disrupt Russian seaborne oil exports and raise tanker/insurance risk premia in the Baltic and beyond.
insights.locator: European deterrence should also mean stricter
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Russia's shadow fleet of oil tankers serves as a crucial financial lifeline for Putin's war machine.
insights.so_what: Targeting oil export logistics is the highest-leverage economic pressure point on Russia.
insights.locator: European deterrence should also mean stricter
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Freezing over $200 billion of Russian Central Bank assets in 2022 has not deterred Kremlin aggression, and several countries are reviving calls for a legal solution to allocate the funds to Ukraine.
insights.so_what: Asset-seizure debate is live again — watch for European legal moves on immobilized reserves.
insights.locator: In addition to targeting the shadow fleet
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Seizing rather than freezing Russian assets would be strongly opposed by Moscow and could destabilize Europe's wider financial system, while airspace and maritime interdiction raise escalation risk — but inaction also emboldens Russia.
insights.so_what: Asset seizure carries reserve-currency and financial-stability implications for the euro system.
insights.quote: Any move to seize rather than freeze Russian assets would be strongly opposed by Moscow and would have the potential to destabilize Europe’s wider financial system.
insights.locator: All these measures carry real risks
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Until Russian hybrid attacks start producing direct strategic losses for Moscow, Putin will continue to escalate.
insights.so_what: Base case is continued gray-zone escalation in Europe absent a policy shift.
insights.quote: Until Russian hybrid attacks on Europe start producing direct strategic losses for Moscow, Putin will continue to escalate.
insights.locator: Europe needs a new counter-hybrid playbook
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
